item.title: How We Taught an AI Model to Understand Documents and Now Onboard New Employees 2x Faster
item.description:
It's strange to talk about a modern tech stack and simultaneously ask new employees to manually enter passport data into an HR form. By automating the onboarding process, we went beyond standard OCR. Based on an LLM VL model, we developed the Sminex Start digital product to manage the onboarding process. Manual labor has been minimized, data stays within the internal network, and new employees understand from day one that they've joined a tech-savvy company. We explain how we achieved this and the benefits we're already seeing in numbers and feedback in this article. LLM vs OCR

item.title: Australian Man on Trial for Leaking Court Documents Using AI
item.description:
Christopher Duff, 40, Sydney, is accused of hacking the NSW court system. Prosecutors allege he used ChatGPT to write a program for downloading sensitive documents. The case involves nearly 9,000 court documents Duff accessed in 2025. He denies the charges, and the court seeks to use his chat logs as evidence, marking a first in Australian justice. Details and arguments from both sides follow.

item.title: Can a data center do without water at all?
item.description:
A slightly experimental format that I hope you'll enjoy. I personally love exploring topics outside of statistics, analytics, and related fields, so sometimes the best way to understand a topic is to try explaining or describing it myself. This material will be about AI, but in a slightly unusual format – we'll try to figure out why data centers are cooled and how they are cooled today, where all the calculations for choosing the right shampoo or spelling "vinaigrette" correctly take place. And behind every such answer are servers, and these servers generate a lot of heat during operation. Read more

item.title: ERP Implemented. What's Next? Part III. From Project-DR to Enterprise-DR
item.description:
This article continues the discussion on ERP implementation, focusing on the transition from the Project-DR development environment to the Enterprise-DR operational model. It defines key terms like Project-DR (Project Digital Replica), Enterprise-DR (Enterprise Digital Replica), and their respective components. The article details how project knowledge is accumulated, how Enterprise-DR is derived from the accepted Project-DR state, what is physically delivered to the client, and how this model is operated post-launch. It emphasizes that Project-DR is an internal technology for building the enterprise model, while Enterprise-DR is the operational, machine-readable replica delivered to the client. The process involves specialized Project Cores, a Unified Project Store, a baseline definition, compilation, and a delivery scrub to ensure only the operational model is transferred, not the underlying technology. The article also touches upon the role of PostgreSQL, Enterprise-DR API, and local LLMs in the operational environment, highlighting the importance of a controlled interface and the distinction between operational history and fundamental model changes that require returning to Project-DR.

item.title: Codebase Intelligence for Agents: Building the "Dev Tool of the Future" and Testing it on a 3.5M+ Line Rails Monolith
item.description:
Over the past year, the number of tools for agent development has exploded, making it easy to get lost. Some promise to maintain context between sessions, others to "understand" the entire codebase, and yet others offer memory, planning, and autonomy in one package. Every week, GitHub repositories appear with impressive (and not always honestly earned) star counts, promising everything at once, only to turn out to be README projects. Others work honestly on demo repositories and crash with OOM at the first encounter with a real enterprise project – and so on, the list can go on. Last fall, I used a combination of Claude + RooCode + semantic search on Ollama, and it was my primary work tool – right up until the combination stopped working (more on that below). I decided to switch entirely to Claude Code and started looking for a replacement for the semantic index, but never found one: alternatives simply didn't work for me – on a 3.5M+ line monolith, they either indexed for hours, required sending code to the cloud (and paying a hefty sum for embeddings!!!), or supported Ruby, to put it mildly, nominally. As a result, I made a difficult decision for myself to create my own tool – starting with a fork of a simple semantic search engine on Ollama + Qdrant – and, characteristically, I succeeded: completely local, so that neither the code nor its derivatives (index, embeddings, call graph) go anywhere. To date, it has taken more than six months (and, I confess, more than a few hundred cups of tea). Read more

item.title: I connected local Gemma to Codex to save on limits. On a simple task, consumption doubled
item.description:
I have a MacBook Pro 16 2019: six-core Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM, and Radeon Pro 5300M with 4 GB VRAM. It already had Ollama, gemma3:4b, and gemma2:2b installed. The idea seemed obvious: why spend cloud Codex on parsing a short traceback, summarizing a log, or a commit message? Let Codex offload such tasks to a local model, get the finished result, and only handle complex tasks. I created an MCP server, connected it to Codex, ran identical tasks, and checked the exact token consumption. The integration worked. Savings - no. On one simple task, the route through the local model used about twice as much cloud input as a direct Codex response. Below is not an instruction on 'how to run a neural network in five minutes,' but an analysis of the experiment: what I built, where I erred in my initial hypothesis, and for what tasks a small local model was still useful. Read on.

item.title: Jev: How its decision API works and what's already being built on it
item.description:
In three days, a small ecosystem has grown around Jev: a browser agent found flight tickets in seven seconds, developers built a trading bot, content filters, and even a Tesla FSD. But Jev doesn't write text. Its API selects an answer from a space pre-defined by the application. I've analyzed the TypeSafe documentation, the jev-ultrafast code, a published trace of a seven-second run, and a hundred primary or near-primary sources. This article covers the Noul, Choice, and Score contract, API calls, pricing, the browser agent's architecture, and 15 early cases with their proof limits. The main question is simple: where does the narrow decision layer truly outperform a standard LLM, and where does a valid answer still turn out to be the wrong answer? Read on
